check:0:0.q: Why not “It runs with 1 worker and never grows”?
check:0:0.a:
That guess sounds reasonable. If you only say the smallest size, it feels natural to assume the cluster stays at that size. And `1` really is the value the team wrote.

But the lesson's rules don't fill in missing sizes. Size must be one of two shapes:

- a fixed `num_workers`, or
- both `min_workers` and `max_workers`, for autoscaling (the cluster adds or removes workers as the load changes).

`min_workers` on its own is neither shape. It is half of the autoscaling pair. So it counts as a problem, just like a raw `policy_id`.

Problems are caught before anything is built. The entry never reaches the plan, so no cluster runs at all, with 1 worker or any other number. Guessing "it stays at 1" means guessing a default the runbook does not have. Reading the plan well means not inventing behaviour the YAML didn't ask for.

"The check rejects it: min and max go together" is better because it names the actual rule: autoscaling needs both limits, and an incomplete size is sent back instead of quietly patched.

check:0:2.q: Why not “The runbook fills in a max_workers for it”?
check:0:2.a:
It's a reasonable guess, because the runbook *does* fill some gaps. If no policy is named, it uses `Personal Compute`. It also builds the final name from the code and name. So "the runbook adds defaults" is true in general.

But size is not one of those defaults. The lesson sets a strict rule: either a fixed `num_workers`, or both `min_workers` and `max_workers` for autoscaling. Autoscaling means Databricks adds or removes workers between a low and a high number. Half a range is not allowed, and the runbook never guesses the missing half.

Look at the runbook line `max_workers = try(c.max_workers, null)`. `try` means "use this value if it exists, otherwise use the fallback." Here the fallback is `null`, which means "nothing." That passes along an empty value. It does not invent a number like 4.

The check also runs first, before anything is built. A cluster with only `min_workers: 1` gets sent back like an incomplete order form.

"The check rejects it: min and max go together" is better because size has no default, and an incomplete autoscaling range is a mistake the check stops before Terraform plans anything.

check:1:1.a:
`MKT_Weekly-Load` gets most of the work right. It puts the code first, then `_`, then the name. It also keeps the `-` in `Weekly-Load`, which is correct. The runbook doesn't touch dashes.

What it misses is the last step. The runbook doesn't just join the two parts. It wraps the joined text in `lower()`, a Terraform function that turns every letter into lower case. So the capitals you typed in the YAML don't survive into the plan.

You can picture it as two steps, in order:

```
join with "_":   MKT_Weekly-Load
lower():         mkt_weekly-load
```

`MKT_Weekly-Load` stops after the first step. It's what you'd get if you only read the YAML. It isn't what Terraform will actually build.

This is the lesson's big idea: predict the plan from the YAML plus the runbook's rules. If the plan showed capitals, that would be a sign something changed in the runbook.

`mkt_weekly-load` is better because it applies both of the runbook's steps: it joins the code and name with `_`, then lower-cases the whole result.

check:1:2.a:
`weekly-load` gets one part right. The runbook does turn the name into **lower case**, so `Weekly-Load` becomes `weekly-load`. That step is correct.

What it misses is the **team code**. The runbook does not use the name from `clusters.yml` on its own. It joins the code and the name with `_`, then lower-cases the whole thing. In the runbook's Terraform, that is this line:

```hcl
name = lower("${c.code}_${c.name}")
```

So for this team:

- `c.code` is `MKT`
- `c.name` is `Weekly-Load`
- joined: `MKT_Weekly-Load`
- lower-cased: `mkt_weekly-load`

The lesson says this prefix is **on purpose**. It is one of the expected differences between what the YAML asked for and what the plan builds. When you read a plan, a cluster named just `weekly-load` would be a surprise. It would mean the code was never added.

`mkt_weekly-load` is better because it follows both runbook steps: code and name joined with `_`, then lower case.

check:2:0.q: Why not “It works: an id is more exact than a name”?
check:2:0.a:
That option gets one thing right. A policy's id does point to exactly one policy. In that narrow sense it is precise.

What it misses is the rule. The question asks what *happens*, not whether an id is a good idea. The lesson says a raw `policy_id` is **not allowed** in `clusters.yml`, so the entry is rejected. However exact the id is, it never reaches the cluster.

It also misses how the runbook is built. Teams give a policy **name** (`policy_name`), or leave it out and get `Personal Compute`. The workspace module then finds the id itself. It does this with `data "databricks_cluster_policy"`, a lookup that reads a policy that already exists rather than creating one. So the id still ends up in the plan. The module fetches it, and the team never writes it.

Here is that difference in YAML:

```yaml
# rejected
policy_id: 0012AB

# allowed
policy_name: Personal Compute
```

"It's rejected: teams name the policy" is better because it states the lesson's rule and says how the id really gets filled in: the module looks it up from the name.

judge.notes: No significant problems. Minor: "it never reaches the cluster" sits awkwardly next to "the id still ends up in the plan" (the first means the team's id, the second the module's looked-up id), and the answer is close to the 200-word limit.

check:2:1.q: Why not “The runbook swaps in Personal Compute”?
check:2:1.a:
That answer gets one thing right. Personal Compute really is the default. When `clusters.yml` names no policy, the runbook fills in Personal Compute, a built-in policy that only makes single-node clusters (one machine, no workers).

But this cluster does not leave the policy out. It gives a raw `policy_id`, and that is not allowed in the YAML at all. Before anything is built, the check walks through the cluster's fields and collects problems. A raw `policy_id` goes on that list. Any problem means the list of problems comes back and no cluster is built. Nothing gets swapped in.

A quiet swap would also be harmful. The team wanted one specific policy. They would silently get a different one, and a cluster that asks for workers would then fail when it is created.

The fix is to name the policy instead. The module then looks up its id with the `databricks_cluster_policy` lookup, so that policy must already exist.

"It's rejected: teams name the policy" is better because it matches the rule: a raw `policy_id` is a problem to send back, not a gap to fill with the default.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

The trouble shows up when you read a plan without first guessing what it should say. A plan is Terraform's list of what it will build. Watch for these in the Spacelift proposed plan:

- **A name you can't explain.** You expected `sales_daily-report` but see something else, such as upper case or a missing code.
- **Personal Compute where you didn't expect it.** The team thought it named a policy, but the default was used. Check that the YAML really names one.
- **A policy lookup error.** The named policy doesn't exist yet. The module only looks policies up. It never creates them.
- **The wrong `can_manage` group,** or none at all, instead of something like `grp-sales-dev-owners`.
- **Rejections you didn't see coming.** These come from a raw `policy_id`, or from a size that mixes `num_workers` with min/max, or gives neither.

**Quickest check**

Before opening the plan, write one line per field from the YAML: name, policy, workers, manager. Then compare it to the plan field by field. For every difference, say whether it is on purpose (the prefix or the default policy) or a mistake. If you can't say which, stop before approving.

judge.notes: Minor: rejections for a raw policy_id or a bad size are validation errors, so they may not appear in the plan itself. The answer is also close to the 200-word limit.

learn:stops.a:
Predicting the plan from the YAML works well, but here are three places where it needs extra care.

**1. The named policy doesn't exist in that workspace.**
The module only *looks up* a policy by name; it never creates one. A policy that exists in DEV may be missing in UAT or PROD, so the plan fails there even though your prediction looked fine. Check the policy exists in each environment's workspace before promoting.

**2. The runbook itself changes.**
Your prediction copies today's rules: the name format, the Personal Compute default, the owner group as manager. If the platform team changes a default in the `locals` block, your mental model goes stale. Re-read the runbook code when a plan surprises you, and treat it as the source of truth.

**3. Stack settings change behaviour.**
Spacelift passes each stack's settings to Terraform as `TF_VAR_` environment variables (values set outside the code). If one of them changes a default or adds access in PROD only, the YAML alone won't show it. Check that stack's settings in the admin repo too.

learn:term.a:
They sound alike, but they do different jobs.

**"Points"** is about *where* things live. `team.yml` doesn't describe the cluster itself. It just says "the cluster details are over in `clusters.yml`." Pointing means holding a reference, like a signpost, not the actual contents.

**"Code"** is a piece of *data*. It's the team's short label, like `SALES`, written inside `clusters.yml` next to the cluster's name and size. The runbook uses it to build the final cluster name.

**How they work together:** the runbook follows the pointer from `team.yml` to find `clusters.yml`. Inside that file it reads the `code`. In the lesson's example, `code: SALES` and `name: daily-report` become `sales_daily-report`.

**An everyday comparison:** think of a filing cabinet. A label on the drawer says "Sales orders are in folder 3." That's pointing. Inside folder 3, each order form has a department stamp reading "SALES." That's the code. The label tells you where to look. The stamp is part of what you find there.

check:0:0.q: Why not “SUPPORTED: the YAML is valid”?
check:0:0.a:
"SUPPORTED: the YAML is valid" gets one thing right. The YAML really is valid. The check (the Pydantic step that rejects unknown fields and wrong types) knows `autotermination_minutes` and accepts the number `30`. So the field gets past the first two stops.

But valid is not the same as SUPPORTED. SUPPORTED means the field reaches the provider as written. The provider is the plugin that actually talks to Databricks.

Here the runbook never reads `autotermination_minutes`. In the lesson's runbook, only `name` and `policy_name` are copied into `dbx_clusters`. Everything else stops there. So the module never sees the field, and the provider never sets it. The cluster in team-sales will not shut itself off after 30 idle minutes, even though the file says it should. The Spacelift plan won't show the setting either. Spacelift is the service that runs Terraform and shows that plan for review.

It's like a parcel with a perfect label that never leaves the sorting office.

"DROPPED: it is accepted but never passed on" is better because it describes what actually happened all the way down, not just whether the file passed the check.

check:0:2.q: Why not “INVALID: the check rejects it”?
check:0:2.a:
"INVALID" gets one thing right: something is wrong with this field. A team wrote `autotermination_minutes: 30` and expected clusters to shut down after 30 idle minutes. That won't happen.

But "INVALID" puts the problem at the wrong stop. INVALID means the check (the Pydantic step) rejected the field. Here the check did the opposite. It allowed the field. So the field got past stop two just fine.

The trouble starts at stop three, the runbook. The runbook only passes on the fields it reads. It never reads `autotermination_minutes`, so the value goes no further:

```hcl
dbx_clusters = [for c in local.clusters : {
  name        = lower("${c.code}_${c.name}")
  policy_name = try(c.policy_name, "Personal Compute")
  # no autotermination_minutes here, so it never reaches the provider
}]
```

That is also why this case is easy to miss. An INVALID field fails loudly at the check. This one fails silently. The YAML looks fine, and the Spacelift plan simply shows no auto-termination setting.

"DROPPED" is the better answer because it says exactly what happened: the field was accepted by the check but never passed on by the runbook, so it does nothing.

judge.notes: No significant problems. Claims like 'fails loudly' and the plan showing no auto-termination setting go slightly past the lesson text but are consistent with it.

check:1:0.q: Why not “SUPPORTED: it arrived exactly as written”?
check:1:0.a:
"SUPPORTED" gets one thing right. The `name` field did reach the provider. The check accepted it, and the runbook passed it on, so it wasn't dropped.

What it misses is the "as written" part. The team wrote `daily-report`. The plan shows `sales_daily-report`. Those are different values, so something changed it on the way down.

That something is the runbook. In the stack's `locals` block, it builds the name like this:

```hcl
name = lower("${c.code}_${c.name}")
```

It puts the team's short code (`sales`) and an underscore in front. Then `lower` makes it all lower case. So the module and provider receive a new value, not the one in the file.

This matters for review. The Spacelift plan is a preview of what would be created, read before anything is applied. A reviewer who knows the field is transformed expects `sales_daily-report` there and won't flag it as a mistake.

"TRANSFORMED: it was changed on the way" is better because it says both things at once: the field reached the provider, and the runbook changed it before it got there.

check:1:2.q: Why not “DEFAULTED: the runbook filled it in”?
check:1:2.a:
"DEFAULTED" gets one thing right. The runbook did step in and add something to the name. The `sales_` prefix was not in the team's YAML. The runbook put it there.

But DEFAULTED means something narrower. It is for a field the team **left out**, so the runbook supplied a whole value of its own. Think of `policy_name`: skip it, and the runbook's `try(...)` drops in `"Personal Compute"`.

That is not what happened here. The team **did** write `name: daily-report`. Their value arrived. It just did not arrive as written. The runbook took it and changed it on the way, using this line:

```hcl
name = lower("${c.code}_${c.name}")
```

This joins the team's short code (`sales`) and their name with an underscore. Then `lower` makes it all lowercase. So `daily-report` becomes `sales_daily-report`. The team's own words are still in there, with a prefix in front.

"TRANSFORMED: it was changed on the way" is the better answer because the team gave a value and the runbook reshaped it, rather than filling in a gap.

check:2:0.q: Why not “SUPPORTED: the check allowed it”?
check:2:0.a:
"SUPPORTED: the check allowed it" gets one thing right. The field passed the check, so it is not INVALID. The Pydantic check found a known field name and a value of the right type.

But passing the check is only stop two of five. The check looks at the YAML file on its own. It has no idea what happens next. SUPPORTED means the field reaches the provider as written, and you haven't looked yet.

The runbook might never pass the field on. Then it is DROPPED: it sits in `clusters.yml`, looks fine, and changes nothing in the Spacelift plan. Or the runbook or module might change it on the way, which makes it TRANSFORMED. You can't tell which until you open the runbook and the module.

Think of the parcel again. A correctly filled-in label doesn't prove it was delivered.

So **UNKNOWN** is the right answer. It honestly says you have only followed the field part of the way, and you need to trace it through the runbook, the module and the provider before you can give it a final word.

check:2:1.q: Why not “DROPPED: nothing uses it yet”?
check:2:1.a:
"DROPPED" gets one thing right. A new field that only the check knows about often *does* end up unused. That is a real risk, and it is good to suspect it.

But you haven't looked yet. You have only seen two stops: the YAML and the check. The runbook (the Terraform code that reads the YAML) and the module (the code that builds the resources) are still unopened. Maybe the runbook passes the field on. Maybe the module uses it. "Nothing uses it" is a claim about places you haven't checked.

DROPPED is a finding. You only earn it by following the field to a stop where it disappears, like a `for` loop in the runbook that never mentions it. Saying it early is a guess dressed up as a fact.

That matters to a reviewer. Someone reading your note next to a Spacelift plan will trust the word you chose. A wrong DROPPED could send a team-sales engineer to "fix" something that already works.

**"UNKNOWN: not traced all the way yet" is better because it honestly says you haven't reached the end, so you can't name the outcome yet.**

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs that a field is being dropped**

- A team edits `clusters.yml`, the check passes, and the Spacelift plan says "no changes." Valid YAML, zero effect. That is the classic sign.
- The cluster in the DEV workspace doesn't match the file. For example, the YAML asks for one policy, but the cluster shows another, or none.
- Support tickets like "I set `autotermination_minutes` weeks ago and nothing happened."
- Reviewers mark a field SUPPORTED, but nobody can point to the provider attribute it ends up in. (An attribute is a named setting on a resource, like `policy_id` on `databricks_cluster`.)
- A setting looks right in DEV but different in UAT or PROD. This can mean a default is quietly filling the gap.

**The quickest check**

Change only that one field in the DEV config. Then open the proposed plan in Spacelift (the preview of changes before anything is applied). If the plan shows that attribute changing, the field reaches the provider. If the plan is empty, the field is dropped somewhere.

Then search the runbook's `locals` for the field name. If it never appears there, you've found where it stops.

judge.notes: No real problems. Minor looseness: 'plan is empty means dropped' ignores a new value that equals the default, and the DEV-vs-UAT/PROD bullet is speculative. The word 'locals' is unexplained, and the answer is close to the 200-word limit.

learn:stops.a:
The rule holds most of the time, but a few situations need extra care.

**The provider gets the field, but Databricks overrides it.** A cluster policy like "Shared Compute - Standard" can fix a setting such as node type, so the value from `clusters.yml` never takes effect. Treat "reaches the provider" as a strong hint, not proof, and confirm in the Spacelift plan or the real workspace.

**The same field behaves differently per environment.** A default can come from a `TF_VAR_` variable (a setting that Spacelift passes into Terraform), and DEV, UAT and PROD stacks may each set it differently. Trace the field once per stage instead of assuming one answer covers all three.

**The runbook passes a whole block through untouched.** If the runbook hands a whole group of settings, such as `custom_tags`, straight to a module, you can't tell from the runbook alone which keys survive. Open the module and follow each key on its own, and mark it UNKNOWN until you do.

judge.notes: No blocking problem. Minor: it calls DEV/UAT/PROD 'stage', but the lesson's setting uses stage for Foundation/Service, and the cluster-policy override point goes beyond the lesson.

learn:term.a:
They answer two different questions. **YAML** is *how* a request is written. The **config repo** is *where* those requests are kept.

**YAML** is a plain-text format for settings. Each line is a name and a value, like `policy_name: Shared Compute - Standard`. Indents show what belongs together. A file such as `clusters.yml` is written in YAML.

The **config repo** is a shared repository. A repository is a folder tracked by Git, a tool that records every change and who made it. Every team's YAML files live there, sorted by environment and team. For example:

```
config/DEV/team-sales/team.yml
config/DEV/team-sales/clusters.yml
```

**How they work together:** team-sales writes its `clusters.yml` in YAML and adds it to the config repo. The runbook then reads that file from the repo. You can see this in the lesson's stack code: `file("${path.module}/config/DEV/team-sales/clusters.yml")`.

**Everyday comparison:** YAML is the order form, and the config repo is the shared office tray where all filled-in forms go. A neatly filled-in form only matters once someone picks it up and acts on it.

check:0:0.q: Why not “CAN_EDIT, because that is what the YAML says”?
check:0:0.a:
That answer gets one thing right. The YAML really does grant `grp-sales-dev-owners` the `CAN_EDIT` level in `folder_grants`. That grant is real, and it does end up in the plan.

What it misses is that the YAML is not the whole story. Because the same group is named as `owner_group`, the runbook (the Terraform root code that reads `team.yml`) adds a second entry you never typed: `grp-sales-dev-owners` with `CAN_MANAGE`.

So the group now appears twice in the folder's access list, once at `CAN_EDIT` and once at `CAN_MANAGE`. A group listed twice does not get both levels, and the first or last entry does not win either. It gets the **highest** of them. The levels, lowest first, are `CAN_READ`, `CAN_RUN`, `CAN_EDIT`, `CAN_MANAGE`. `CAN_MANAGE` sits above `CAN_EDIT`.

Reading only the YAML would make the plan look wrong when it is actually correct.

"`CAN_MANAGE`, the higher of the two" is better because it counts the owner access the runbook adds and then keeps the highest level for a group that shows up twice.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Both, as two separate permissions”?
check:0:2.a:
"Both, as two separate permissions" gets one thing right. The list the runbook builds really does name `grp-sales-dev-owners` twice. Once is the `CAN_MANAGE` the runbook adds for the owner. The other is the `CAN_EDIT` typed in `team.yml`. So if you only read the list, "both" looks reasonable.

What it misses is what the folder does with that list. A group has one **effective** permission on a folder. Effective means the level that actually applies when someone tries to do something. When a group shows up twice, it keeps the **highest** of its levels, not a pile of separate ones.

The levels also stack, lowest first: `CAN_READ`, `CAN_RUN`, `CAN_EDIT`, `CAN_MANAGE`. Each one includes everything below it. `CAN_MANAGE` can already do everything `CAN_EDIT` can, and more. So a separate `CAN_EDIT` would add nothing.

That's why, in review, you check who ends up with what, not how many lines the list has.

"CAN_MANAGE, the higher of the two" is better because it describes the single level the group actually ends up with on the folder.

judge.notes: No major problems. The claim that each level includes everything below it is an inference from the lesson's lowest-first ordering rather than something the lesson states outright.

check:1:0.q: Why not “It's a mistake: take it out of the plan”?
check:1:0.a:
"It's a mistake: take it out of the plan" starts from a good instinct. A reviewer should question access nobody asked for. Spotting that `team.yml` never mentions `users` is careful reading.

But it misses where that line comes from. The runbook adds it on purpose. In the `folder_access` local, after the owner group and the explicit grants, it always appends `users` at `CAN_READ`. `users` is the built-in group holding everyone in the workspace. So the plan is doing exactly what the code says. Nothing went wrong.

"Take it out of the plan" also doesn't work as a fix. The plan is only Terraform's preview of changes, built from the code and the YAML. You can't edit one line of it. To drop that grant, you'd have to change the runbook itself. That changes the default for every team, not just `team-sales`. That's a platform decision, not a review comment.

"It's expected: the runbook adds it" is better because it traces the access to its real source and checks who ends up with what, instead of assuming the plan invented it.

check:1:2.q: Why not “It's a leak: someone edited it by hand”?
check:1:2.a:
**Why "It's a leak: someone edited it by hand" isn't the best answer**

It does get one thing right. Spotting access that nobody typed in `team.yml` and asking where it came from is a good habit. Access you can't explain is worth a question.

What it misses is where that access actually comes from. The runbook (the Terraform root code that reads the YAML) adds access on its own. It gives the owner group `CAN_MANAGE` and every workspace user `CAN_READ` by default. You can see the second rule in the stack's code:

```hcl
[{ group_name = "users", permission_level = "CAN_READ" }],
```

That line is part of `local.folder_access`. So `users` getting `CAN_READ` is written into the runbook itself. You don't need a hand edit to explain it.

Calling it a leak skips the lesson's key step. Before you call something a mistake, check what the runbook adds. Then review who ends up with what.

**Why "It's expected: the runbook adds it" is better:** it names the real source, the runbook's default for every workspace user, so the reviewer can confirm it in the code instead of guessing.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Yes: the first group listed wins”?
check:2:0.a:
**"Yes: the first group listed wins"** gets one thing right. It notices that something has to decide what happens when a list could say different things about a group.

But it picks the wrong rule. Position in the list never decides access. When a group appears twice, it ends up with the **highest** of its levels. For example, `CAN_EDIT` beats `CAN_READ`, wherever each one sits in the list.

It also misses what this question describes. Both plans give the same groups the same permissions. A **plan** is Terraform's preview of what it will change. Here, the order is the only difference. Databricks applies the whole set of grants on the folder together, so it doesn't read them top to bottom. Two lists with the same pairs, like `grp-sales-dev-owners` with `CAN_MANAGE` and `users` with `CAN_READ`, leave the folder in exactly the same state. Flagging that would send the team chasing a change that does nothing.

**"No: only who ends up with what matters"** is better because a reviewer's job is to check the final access each group gets, and that is identical in both plans.

judge.notes: No real problem. The line about Databricks applying grants together goes slightly beyond the lesson, but it fits the lesson's 'review who ends up with what, not the order'.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Yes: it must match the order in team.yml”?
check:2:1.a:
It's a reasonable instinct. You want the plan to reflect what the team asked for in `team.yml`. That part is right.

But order isn't what the team asked for. They asked for access. A folder's permissions work like a guest list, not a queue. Databricks checks whether a group is on the list and at what level. Whether `grp-sales-dev-analysts` appears first or third changes nothing about what it can do.

The plan (Terraform's preview of the changes it will make) also can't match `team.yml` order anyway. The runbook builds the list itself. It puts the owner group at `CAN_MANAGE` first, then the explicit `folder_grants`, then `users` at `CAN_READ` last. Two of those entries aren't in `team.yml` at all. So "must match the order" would flag nearly every plan, even correct ones.

Flagging order wastes the reviewer's attention on noise. It also pulls focus from the real question: did any group end up with a level it shouldn't have?

"No: only who ends up with what matters" is better because each group's final permission level is what controls access to the folder, and the order of the list never does.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs the idea was skipped**

- **"Mystery" permissions in review.** Someone flags `CAN_MANAGE` on `grp-sales-dev-owners` as a bug, even though `team.yml` never asked for it. The runbook added it. Nothing went wrong.
- **"Fixes" that fight the runbook.** A teammate edits `team.yml` to remove the "extra" access. The next Spacelift plan shows it again, because the runbook adds it every run.
- **Wrong levels after apply.** A group listed twice shows the *lower* level. Or a group ends up with two entries. Either way, the highest-wins rule was missed.
- **Noise about order.** A review comment complains that entries moved around. Order doesn't matter. Only who ends up with what matters.
- **Surprise lockouts.** Workspace users can't open notebooks under `/Teams/team-sales` because the default `CAN_READ` for `users` went missing.

**Quickest check**

Before reading the plan, write a short "expected" list, one line per group:

- Start with what `team.yml` asks for.
- Add what the runbook adds.
- Where a group appears twice, keep only its higher level.

Then compare your list to the plan's folder permissions, group by group. Any group that differs is where to look.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Someone clicks access in by hand.** `databricks_permissions` is authoritative: it treats its list as the complete truth for that folder. A grant added in the Databricks screen is "drift" (a change made outside the code), and the next apply removes it. Ask the team to add it to `folder_grants` in `team.yml` instead.

**2. The default `CAN_READ` for `users` is too open.** That default fits most DEV folders. A PROD folder for team-sales may hold things not every workspace user should see. Make the default a per-environment or per-team setting rather than always adding it, and review it in the plan.

**3. Access comes from somewhere else too.** Everything inside a folder inherits its levels, so a grant on a parent folder like `/Teams` also reaches `/Teams/team-sales`. Then the plan for this one folder doesn't show everyone's real access. Check the parent folders' permissions as well when you answer "who ends up with what."

judge.notes: Point 1 (authoritative permissions and drift) goes beyond what the lesson states, but it is accurate and doesn't contradict the lesson.

learn:term.a:
"Highest" means the most powerful of the four permission levels.

Think of passes for an office building. A lobby pass gets you through the front door. A staff pass also opens the offices. A manager pass opens every room and lets you hand out passes. If someone is given two passes, they don't need both. They just use the stronger one, because it already covers everything the weaker one does.

Folder permissions work the same way. Lowest first: `CAN_READ`, `CAN_RUN`, `CAN_EDIT`, `CAN_MANAGE`. Each level includes what the ones below it allow. So `CAN_MANAGE` is the highest.

In the lesson's example, the runbook gives `grp-sales-dev-owners` `CAN_MANAGE` because it is the owner group. Now suppose `team.yml` also listed that same group under `folder_grants` with `CAN_EDIT`. The group is named twice. It ends up with `CAN_MANAGE`, the higher of the two. It doesn't get both, and the lower one doesn't win.

That's why a plan can show a stronger level than the YAML asked for. Check what the runbook adds before calling it a mistake.

judge.notes: Minor: it says each level includes everything below it, which the lesson never states, and it opens with a one-line definition before the everyday comparison. Neither contradicts the lesson.

check:0:1.a:
"The runbook" gets one thing right. The runbook is where clusters actually get built. Its Terraform (code that describes infrastructure) reads each team's YAML and creates what it asks for. So team-hr's new cluster will pass through the runbook.

But the runbook answers a different question: how does YAML become an environment? Its code is shared by every team. If you added team-hr's cluster there, you would mix one team's wish into the rules for everyone. Other teams' plans would run through that edit too. And team-hr's folder would no longer show everything team-hr has.

The request answers "what does one team want?" That question lives in the config repo. You would add the cluster to `clusters.yml` in team-hr's folder. Pydantic (a library that checks each field has the right shape) validates it. Then the runbook picks it up on its next run, with no change to its own code.

The config repo is better because a request for one team belongs in that team's folder, and the runbook already knows how to build it.

judge.notes: No significant problems; 'where clusters actually get built' is slightly loose, since the runbook calls modules, but it does not contradict the lesson.

check:0:2.a:
"The workspace module" has one thing right. A cluster runs inside a workspace, so the module is close to where the cluster ends up.

But look at the question the module answers: what is one workspace? It is shared Terraform code. Every workspace is built from it. If you edit it, you change things for every team, not just team-hr. A module change also needs a new release with a version number, like `v1.4.0`. Then the runbook has to bump to that version. That is a lot of work and risk for one cluster.

This request is a team's wish: team-hr wants one more cluster in DEV. "What does a team want?" is the config repo's question. The change goes in team-hr's folder, in its `clusters.yml` file. Pydantic, a tool that checks each field, validates it. The runbook then reads that YAML, adds its defaults and access rules, and calls the modules as it always does.

"The config repo" is better because the change is for one team, and one team's wishes live in that team's folder.

check:1:0.a:
It's a fair guess. `clusters.yml` is where a team describes its clusters, so editing it would give those clusters a 20-minute auto-stop. (Auto-stop means a cluster shuts itself down after sitting idle, which saves money.)

But look at the question each repo answers. The config repo answers "what does a team want?" Each `clusters.yml` holds one team's own choices. A rule for every team is a different question: "what does every team get by default?" That question lives in the runbook.

Putting it in every `clusters.yml` causes real problems:

- **Lots of edits.** You'd change `team-sales`, then every other team folder, one by one.
- **New teams miss it.** A team added next month starts without the 20-minute setting unless someone remembers.
- **It drifts.** A team could delete the line, and nothing would put it back.
- **It's not your file.** Those folders hold each team's requests, not platform-wide rules.

The runbook is better because it adds defaults to every team's YAML in one place, so every current and future team gets the 20-minute auto-stop automatically.

judge.notes: The 'drifts' and 'not your file' bullets go slightly beyond the lesson, but they are reasonable and do not contradict it.

check:1:2.a:
"The admin repo" is a fair guess. It does reach every team. Its stack settings flow into Terraform as `TF_VAR_` environment variables, and its policies check every plan. So it feels like the place for "applies to everyone."

But look at the question each repo answers. The admin repo answers "how do runs happen?" It holds Spacelift's stacks (one stack runs one stage of Terraform), their settings, and policies. A policy is a rule that approves or blocks a plan. It can say "reject clusters without auto-stop." It cannot fill in the 20 minutes for you.

An auto-stop of 20 minutes is about *what gets built*, not *how the run happens*. It is a default: a value every team gets unless they ask for something else. Adding defaults to each team's YAML is exactly the runbook's job. Putting it in the admin repo would hide a build decision inside run settings, where nobody reading the Terraform would find it.

"The runbook" is better because it is where every team's YAML gets its defaults before the modules are called.

judge.notes: Minor: "adding defaults to each team's YAML" could be read as editing the config repo, when the runbook adds defaults as it reads the YAML; the `TF_VAR_` mention is also unexplained for beginners.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Every team updates its YAML”?
check:2:1.a:
"Every team updates its YAML" points at the wrong repo and the wrong step.

**What it gets right:** team YAML does feed the runbook. If the new setting were something each team picks for itself, a team folder might one day hold a value for it.

**What it misses:** the config repo answers "what does a team want?" This change answers "what is one workspace?", and that question lives in the module repo. The runbook calls the module at a fixed version, like `?ref=v1.4.0`. If the new input only exists in unreleased module code, the runbook can't pass it. No YAML edit changes that. A setting every workspace needs is also a default, so the runbook supplies it. Teams shouldn't each have to remember it.

So the order is:

1. Change the module.
2. Release a new version, say `v1.5.0`.
3. In the runbook, bump `?ref=v1.4.0` to `?ref=v1.5.0` and pass the new value.

Each step gets its own reviewed pull request, in that order.

**Why "A new module version is released" is better:** the runbook can only use what a released module version offers, so the release has to come first.

check:2:2.a:
It's a fair guess. Spacelift does run everything, and the admin repo does control those runs. So "something has to run" is not wrong in spirit.

But the admin stack answers a different question: how do runs happen? Running it updates Spacelift's own setup, such as its stacks, policies and each stack's settings. It never touches the workspace module's code. After it runs, the runbook still can't see your new input.

The real blocker is versioning. The runbook doesn't use the module's latest code. It pins one released version with `?ref=`, a tag like `v1.4.0` written into the module's source address. Your new input only exists in code that isn't in any release yet. So if the runbook passes that input while still pinned to `v1.4.0`, Terraform fails with an "unsupported argument" error.

The order is:

1. Change the module.
2. Release a new version, say `v1.5.0`.
3. Bump `?ref=` in the runbook and pass the new value.

"A new module version is released" is better because a release is the only thing that makes the new input exist at a version the runbook can point to.

judge.notes: No real problems; the 'unsupported argument' error detail is not in the lesson, but it is accurate Terraform behavior and it does not contradict the lesson.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
When a change lands in the wrong repo, the signs usually show up in Spacelift plans and pull requests.

- **A plan touches more than expected.** You asked for one thing for `team-sales`, but the plan (Terraform's preview of what it will change) shows edits in every workspace. A one-team request went into the runbook or a module.
- **The same edit repeats across team folders.** Copying a default into `team-sales`, `team-hr` and others means it belonged once in the runbook.
- **The runbook rejects a new input.** Terraform says the module has no such argument. The module wasn't released yet, or `?ref=` still points at the old version.
- **A rule lives in the wrong place.** "Block catalog deletes" written into runbook code isn't a plan policy. It belongs in the admin repo.
- **Someone edited identities, PROD access or state.** That needed the platform owner.

Quickest check: read the pull request and say which question it answers. One team, every team, every workspace, or how runs happen? If the repo doesn't match that question, it's in the wrong place.

learn:stops.a:
**When the rule needs extra care**

**1. A change answers two questions at once.** Say every team should get a new default, but the module has no input for it yet. Split it into ordered pull requests: change the module, release a version, then bump `?ref=` in the runbook and pass the value.

**2. A team request hides a risky part.** A `team.yml` change for `team-sales` might look like a config repo job, but it could also ask for `sp-sales-etl-prod` with PROD access. Check for risk before checking scope, and send anything about identities, PROD or state to the platform owner, with the details written down.

**3. The same "one team" change keeps repeating.** If many team folders copy the same setting, such as `CAN_RUN` for an owner group, it has really become an "every team" question. Move it into the runbook as a default, so one rule replaces many copies.

In each case, the idea still holds. You just ask the question more carefully.

learn:term.a:
Think of a restaurant kitchen. A customer's order says what they want. The kitchen's recipe book says how to turn any order into a finished plate, including the parts every plate gets, like salt and a garnish.

In this lesson, the **runbook** is that recipe book. It is Terraform "root code", meaning the top-level Terraform that actually gets run. It reads each team's YAML from the config repo. It adds the defaults and access rules every team should get. Then it calls the workspace and catalog modules to build the real environment.

It works in stages. `Foundation` handles account-level setup. `Service` handles each workspace. Spacelift runs each stage as a "stack", which is one separately run piece of Terraform.

You'll see it twice in the example:

- "Every team folder gets `CAN_RUN`" goes to the runbook. That is a default rule applied to every team, not one team's wish.
- After a module change, you "bump `?ref=`" in the runbook. That means updating the module version number the runbook points to.

Outside this course, "runbook" often means a written step-by-step guide. Here it means this code.
